                    April 30, 2026

## Sprites API

### Improved: Storage sync jobs are now resilient to deploys

Large storage syncs are now broken into a chain of small jobs, one per page of buckets, instead of one long-running job. This means a rolling deploy no longer forces a full re-sync from scratch — each page finishes well within the deployment grace period and any interrupted page is safely retried without producing duplicate billing records.

### Improved: Remote MCP server tools are clearer and safer

The Sprites remote MCP server now exposes metadata that lets Claude distinguish read-only tools from destructive ones. Users also get more actionable error messages when required parameters are missing or a backend routing issue occurs.

### Improved: Storage sync resumes from where it failed

If a storage sync job hits an error partway through paginating buckets, it now picks up from the point of failure instead of starting over from the beginning. Buckets already processed are not lost, and a follow-up job is automatically queued to continue from the last successful offset.

### Fixed: Oban queue stats were silently failing to report

A type mismatch in the queue stats query was causing an error on every poll, which meant job queue metrics ( sprites_oban_queue_stats_count ,  oldest_age_ms ) were never emitted to Prometheus. The query now runs correctly and metrics appear as expected.

### Fixed: Empty job queues now report zero instead of disappearing from metrics

When a job queue drained completely, its metrics series would vanish from Prometheus rather than showing zero. Queue stats now explicitly emit a zero value for every tracked state, so dashboards and alerts behave correctly even when queues are empty.

### Improved: Prometheus metrics are now active in production

The Prometheus metrics endpoint is now enabled in the application’s supervision tree. Metrics were previously collected but not served; they are now available and scraped in production.

### Fixed: Metrics server no longer fails to start during blue/green deploys

The Prometheus metrics listener previously crashed with an address-in-use error when a new instance started before the old one finished shutting down during a blue/green deploy. The server now uses socket options that allow both instances to bind the same port simultaneously during the cutover window.

                    April 28, 2026

## Sprites API

### New: Prometheus metrics for background job queues

The Sprites API now exposes Prometheus metrics for its internal job pipeline, including job durations, error rates, and queue depths per queue. This makes it possible to set up precise alerts and dashboards using PromQL instead of fragile log-string matching.

### Improved: Cleaned up completed backfill infrastructure

The temporary backfill queue and workers used to rebuild app index records have been removed now that the backfill is complete. This keeps the job pipeline tidy and reduces overhead.

### Fixed: Storage sync errors for non-active sprites

Storage sync was skipping app index records for destroyed or archived sprites, causing thousands of “AppRecord not found” errors every hour. The fix ensures all sprites — regardless of status — are covered, eliminating the recurring error noise.

### Improved: Reduced log noise from orphaned storage buckets

Missing app record warnings during storage sync are now logged at warning level instead of error level, with a single batch summary instead of one error per bucket. Real storage sync failures are now much easier to spot in the logs.

### Improved: Increased SQLite queue timeouts

Internal SQLite queue timeouts have been bumped to better handle bursts of activity without triggering premature timeout failures.

### Improved: Faster, more reliable health probes and self-replay requests

Health probes and internal self-replay requests now use a larger dedicated connection pool (50x4 instead of 50x1), reducing connection checkout timeouts when many sprite channels are active at the same time.

                    April 21, 2026

## Sprites API

### New: Control who can access private sprite URLs

You can now set  private_access  on a sprite’s URL settings to allow all org members — not just admins — to access private sprite URLs. The default remains admin-only. Admins can view and change this setting from the sprite detail page.

### Fixed: Storage usage was being recorded for deleted sprites

A background job was incorrectly tracking storage usage for sprites that had already been deleted, causing phantom billing data to accumulate. Deleted sprites are now correctly identified and skipped during storage accounting.

### Improved: Remote MCP server tools are clearer and safer

The Sprites remote MCP server now exposes metadata that lets Claude distinguish read-only tools from destructive ones. Users also get more actionable error messages when required parameters are missing or a backend routing issue occurs.

## Sprites Go SDK

### New: Labels support

You can now set, update, and clear labels on sprites using the Go SDK. The new types and helpers integrate with sprite create and update flows.

 [PR #18](https://github.com/superfly/sprites-go/pull/18)

### New: PrivateAccess field in URLSettings

The Go SDK’s  URLSettings  struct now includes a  PrivateAccess  field, supporting the new sprite URL access control option. This change is backward compatible with older servers.

 [PR #17](https://github.com/superfly/sprites-go/pull/17)

                    April 16, 2026

## Sprites API

# Stateful sandbox environments

 with checkpoint & restore

        A Sprite is a
        [hardware-isolated execution environment](https://fly.io/sprites/#sandbox-vms)
        for arbitrary code: a persistent Linux computer. Whether it's an AI agent like Claude Code or a binary your user just uploaded, Sprites are the simplest answer for "where should I run a blob of code".

## Persistence

- ### Tiered storage

 You read and write to a fast, directly-attached NVMe filesystem that continuously syncs to durable, external object storage.
- ### Same disk for every run

 Your files, installs, and data are on the same paths every run; the environment comes back exactly as you left it.
- ### Max compatibility

 It's a standard ext4 filesystem, so anything that reads or writes to disk just works, no special API or SDK.
- ### Automatically grows

 The disk is thin-provisioned up to 100 GB; it grows as you write instead of being pre-allocated, so you never size or resize a volume.
- ### Only pay for actual data

 You're billed for the bytes you actually write, not a reserved size, and because the filesystem is TRIM-friendly, deleting files lowers your bill.

## Checkpoints

- ### Live checkpoints

 Checkpoints are transactional metadata. They take about 300ms and your Sprite environment won't even notice.
- ### Copy-On-Write

 Runs copy-on-write, capturing only what changed, so a checkpoint is fast and doesn't interrupt the running Sprite.
- ### Full environment

 Captures your whole writable filesystem, meaning every file, package, and on-disk database you've added on top of the base image, not just one directory.
- ### Quick restores

 Restore to any checkpoint in moments to roll the filesystem back to that exact point.
- ### Manage them within the environment

 Create, list, and restore checkpoints from inside the Sprite via the sprite-env CLI or the management API.

## Sprite URLs

- ### URLs for external access

 Every Sprite has its own independent URL for reaching services running inside it.
- ### Activate sprite

 An incoming request to a Sprite's URL wakes it automatically, so it's ready to serve even after it has paused.
- ### Just listen on 8080

 Bind your app to port 8080 and the proxy routes public traffic straight to it, no extra config.
- ### Public access, if you want

 Keep a URL private to your org, or flip it fully public to the internet with a single setting.

## Sandbox VMs

- ### Disposable compute

 The VM behind a Sprite is disposable: it spins up when there's work to do and is released when the Sprite goes idle. Your environment persists regardless, so a Sprite you haven't touched in months boots right back up when you return.
- ### Firecracker VMs

 Each Sprite runs in a hardware-isolated Firecracker microVM, not a shared container.
- ### Isolated networking

 Each Sprite runs on its own isolated network, separate from every other tenant.
- ### Dynamic resources

 A Sprite can burst up to 8 vCPUs, its memory grows automatically under load, and it pauses entirely when idle, so you pay for real usage.

## Network Policy

- ### Fine-grained network egress

 Egress is controlled by a policy of allowed and denied domains; a Sprite can only reach the destinations you permit.
- ### Simple rules

 A short JSON allow/deny list of domains, with a built-in defaults set for common dev services (GitHub, npm, PyPI, AI APIs).
- ### Live updates via REST API

 Push new rules through the Sprite API and they reload automatically; connections to newly-blocked domains drop, with no restart.
- ### Transparent to applications

 Enforcement happens at the network layer with no proxy in the path, so your app needs no code changes or special configuration.

At this size, use four persistent project sandboxes. Each project sandbox can hold three Git worktrees. Twelve separate persistent VMs add cost without improving tenant isolation.

I used these assumptions:

- Two users with two projects each.
- Twelve workstream sessions daily.
- Each session uses one active hour.
- Monthly active time is 360 sandbox-hours.
- Each project stores 10 GB, giving 40 GB total.
- Fixed-size sandboxes receive 2 vCPUs and 2 GB RAM.
- Prices exclude model APIs, Yinshi control-plane hosting, logs, and outbound traffic.

## Estimated monthly execution cost

| Platform | Monthly estimate | Calculation |
|---|---:|---|
| **Fly Sprites Level 20** | **About $20** | Average provider example usage consumes about 216 CPU-hours and 540 GB-memory-hours. The $20 plan publishes allowances of 450 CPU-hours, 1,800 GB-memory-hours, and 50 GB-months. |
| **Fly Machines** | **About $15–$20** | About $6 compute, $6 volumes, and roughly $4 for stopped root files plus snapshots. |
| **AWS Fargate** | **About $32–$40** | About $18 compute, $12 EFS storage, $2 public IPv4, then modest logging charges. |
| **AWS Fargate with NAT** | **About $65–$80** | A single NAT gateway adds about $32 monthly before data processing. Stronger managed outbound controls can cost more. |
| **E2B Pro** | **About $198** | $150 base fee plus about $48 usage. The usage estimate assumes 2 vCPUs and 2 GB RAM. Storage fits within the included 20 GB per sandbox. |
| **Self-hosted Kata or Firecracker** | **At least $150–$400** | Production needs several KVM hosts, backups, networking, and operator time. Two users cannot amortize that platform yet. |

For E2B, one active hour costs about $0.133 at 2 vCPUs and 2 GB RAM. The free Hobby plan removes the $150 base fee, but its one-hour limit is unsuitable for production.

Sprites usage without plan credits would cost about $41 monthly. The published $20 Level 20 allowance covers this workload under the stated utilization assumptions. Confirm current allowances in the Sprites dashboard before committing.

Fargate uses 1 vCPU and 2 GB in the estimate because its supported sizes differ. Its compute rate is about $0.049 per active hour. EFS Standard storage costs $0.30 per GB-month in `us-east-1`.

## Session-length sensitivity

| Active time per workstream | Monthly sandbox-hours | Sprites usage before plan credits | E2B Pro | Fargate compute only |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 30 minutes | 180 | $21 | $174 | $9 |
| 1 hour | 360 | $41 | $198 | $18 |
| 2 hours | 720 | $81 | $246 | $36 |

The Sprites $20 plan still fits the two-hour case under the provider example’s average CPU and memory use. Heavy builds can exceed its included CPU allowance.

## Branch lifecycle changes everything

If twelve new environments remain stored every day, month-end count reaches 360. Average retained storage becomes roughly 1.8 TB-month at 10 GB each.

That retention pattern adds about $540 monthly on EFS Standard. Fly volumes add about $270 before root files and snapshots. Sprites cold storage adds about $35 above its included storage.

Keep one sandbox per project instead. Put each branch in a Git worktree, then delete old worktrees under a retention policy.

## Recommendation

For two users, Sprites has the best cost and workspace fit. Fly Machines cost slightly less, but Yinshi must implement more network and lifecycle controls.

Fargate is reasonable when AWS control matters more than startup speed. E2B Pro is difficult to justify at this user count. Self-hosted Firecracker becomes economical only after much higher sustained usage.

- Test backup restoration.

Confirm Fly’s encryption terms before loading user data. Encrypt external backups with Yinshi-managed keys.

E2B Pro adds a $150 monthly base fee. Fly Machines save only a few dollars while shifting more security work into Yinshi. Fargate costs more after persistent storage and managed outbound routing.

Start with trial credits. Activate Level 20 when daily use begins.
How to we integrate sprites into the project? Which files do we need to focus on?

name: coding-practices
description: Applies implementation and review standards for completeness, validation, control flow, naming, comments, error handling, state, explicit options, and testing. Use before writing, modifying, refactoring, or reviewing code in any language.
---

# Coding Practices

Follow more specific repository conventions when they differ. Apply every relevant rule below.

## Completeness

Deliver complete behavior at the repository's quality bar. A release may omit features, but existing behavior must be sound. Do not leave TODOs, placeholder implementations, or temporary shortcuts. If work cannot be completed now, open an issue instead of leaving an unactionable comment.

## Assertions and Defensive Checks

Validate data at function boundaries. Use assertions for programmer errors and explicit exceptions for user or external input.

Pair checks across related paths. Validate data before writing it to a store and validate it again after reading it back. Check both what must be true and what must not be true, especially at valid-invalid boundaries.

Aim for at least two assertions or defensive checks in each behavior-bearing function. A function without checks should only wire calls together or delegate work.

## Control Flow

Use direct control flow and extract helpers before nesting becomes difficult to follow. Split compound conditions when each branch needs to be independently clear.

Consider whether an `else` should document the unhandled path. State invariants positively, such as `index < length`, rather than through negated boundary checks. Keep function bodies near 50 lines; longer functions usually contain more than one responsibility.

## Naming

Choose exact nouns and verbs that give the reader the correct mental model. Do not abbreviate names when the full term is clearer. Prefer names such as `source`, `target`, and `message_count` over `src`, `dst`, and `msg_cnt`.

Place units and qualifiers after the main noun, such as `latency_ms_max`, so related names sort together. Prefer paired names with similar length, and do not reuse one term for different meanings across subsystems.

## Comments and Documentation

Comments should explain why a choice exists so a reader can judge the tradeoff. Put a short description at the top of each test file that states the covered behavior and how the tests check it. Write comments as complete sentences; brief inline labels are acceptable.

## Error Handling

Handle every signaled error. Do not use a bare catch. Catch a broad exception only when the handler logs and re-raises, translates it into a meaningful domain error, or completely handles the failure. Trace each failure path, and make every caller deal explicitly with failures it can receive.

## Scope and State

Keep state small and local. Declare variables close to first use. Do not duplicate state that can drift from its source. Keep few variables alive at once so misuse remains easy to detect.

## Explicit Options

Spell out options at call sites when defaults affect behavior. Be explicit about encoding, timeouts, sort order, and other settings whose defaults could change or hide intent.

## Testing

The usual stack is Python backends with static HTML and JSON or YAML configuration, but repository conventions control. When adding functionality, update coupled test expectations such as tool or test counts. Run the full test suite after code changes.

name: software-design
description: Applies principles from "A Philosophy of Software Design" to architecture, module and API boundaries, and consequential refactors. Use for architecture planning, module or API design, design review, or diagnosing shallow modules, information leakage, and pass-through layers.
---

# Software Design

Apply these principles when architecture or abstraction quality is a material part of the task.

## Two Modes

### Writing New Code

Apply these principles in order of impact.

#### Think strategically

Invest in design instead of stopping when the code first works. Produce a clean design that works, and spend 10–20% of the effort on design improvements.

#### Create deep modules

Each module should provide powerful functionality behind a simple interface. A few deep methods beat many shallow ones. Ask whether the interface is simpler than the implementation.

#### Hide information

Each module should encapsulate design decisions that remain invisible through its interface. If one decision appears in several modules, reorganize the code until that decision has one home.

#### Make interfaces general-purpose

Design an interface broad enough to support current uses while keeping its functionality focused. Ask for the simplest interface that covers every current need.

#### Give each layer a different abstraction

Adjacent layers should operate at different abstraction levels. Remove pass-through methods that delegate with the same signature.

#### Pull complexity downwards

Handle complexity inside the module instead of pushing it to callers. A simple interface matters more than a simple implementation.

#### Define errors out of existence

Redefine APIs so avoidable error conditions cannot arise. Mask low-level exceptions and consolidate their handling. Reserve crashes for unrecoverable failures.

#### Design it twice

Consider at least two radically different approaches before committing. Compare their strengths and costs. Apply this comparison to interfaces and implementations, then consider the broader system decomposition.

#### Name precisely

Names should create a clear mental image of an entity's purpose. Avoid vague choices such as `data`, `result`, `info`, or `tmp`. Name booleans with predicates such as `isConnected` instead of a state label such as `status`.

#### Be consistent

Use the same name for the same purpose everywhere. Reuse established coding patterns and conventions. Consistency reduces the reader's cognitive work.

#### Make code obvious

Code is obvious when a reader's first guess about its behaviour is correct. Choose precise names and follow established patterns. Use whitespace to expose structure, and comment only where the code cannot explain itself.

#### Write comments first

Write interface comments before implementation. A method that needs a long descriptive comment has a complex interface and should be redesigned. Comments should preserve information that code cannot represent.

### Reviewing Existing Code

Scan for these red flags in the listed order.

#### Shallow modules

Look for interfaces as complex as their implementations, many trivial methods, or classes with little functionality.

#### Information leakage

Find design decisions repeated across modules. A change to one detail should not require coordinated edits across several classes.

#### Temporal decomposition

Check for code organized around operation order instead of information hiding, such as separate read and write classes for one format.

#### Pass-through methods

Flag methods that only call another method with the same signature, especially when delegation accounts for half or more of a class's methods.

#### Overexposure

A common operation should not force callers to understand rare features. Default information that callers should not have to provide.

#### Conjoined methods

Flag a method when understanding it requires reading another method's implementation.

#### Repetition

Find non-trivial code patterns duplicated in several places.

#### Vague or hard-to-pick names

Flag names broad enough to describe many entities. Difficulty finding a precise name often means the entity has too many responsibilities.

#### Comment problems

Find comments that restate the code or expose implementation details in interface documentation. Long, complicated descriptions may reveal a poor abstraction.

#### Special-general mixture

Keep specialized use-case code out of a general-purpose mechanism.

#### Nonobvious code

Flag behaviour that a quick reading cannot reveal, including surprising side effects.

#### Too many exceptions

Look for exceptions the caller cannot handle and error paths longer than the normal path. Redefine operations when doing so can eliminate error conditions.

For the full checklist, read `references/red-flags.md`.

## References

`references/principles.md` covers all 15 design principles. It includes examples and techniques, along with the reasoning behind each principle. Read it when applying a specific principle or when deeper context is needed.

`references/red-flags.md` organizes every red flag by category. Read it during code review to check systematically for design problems.

name: grill-for-unknowns
description: Grills complex implementation plans against source evidence to expose material unknowns before coding. Use for unfamiliar code or APIs, vague product direction, consequential architecture, failed assumption-driven work, or long-running agent handoffs.
license: MIT
---

# Grill for Unknowns

Use the gap between map and territory to find decisions that could invalidate a build.

| Concept | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Map | The request, plan, assumptions, prior context, and current mental model. |
| Territory | The codebase, documentation, tests, APIs, deployment environment, product constraints, user taste, and failure modes. |
| Material unknown | An unresolved fact or decision that could change architecture, scope, user experience, data, security, permissions, cost, or acceptance criteria. |

Stay in exploration or planning until every material unknown is resolved or recorded as an explicit assumption. Begin implementation only after the user confirms the shared understanding or authorizes work under those assumptions.

Skip this process for mechanical tasks with clear acceptance criteria. When one tool call can settle the issue, inspect the territory and act on the result instead of opening an interview.

## Procedure

### 1. Reconstruct the map

Restate the requested outcome, current plan, stated constraints, and existing artifacts. Separate user statements from agent assumptions. For a complex session, open [`templates/grill-session.md`](templates/grill-session.md) and maintain it as the working ledger.

Finish this step when the desired outcome is concrete enough to test and every inferred constraint is labeled as an assumption.

### 2. Inspect the territory

Read the relevant source, tests, configuration, schemas, migrations, logs, issue history, and official documentation before asking questions. Examine similar in-repository implementations and any reference implementation supplied by the user. Fetch retrievable evidence; mark inaccessible evidence and dependent claims as unverified.

Facts belong to evidence gathering. Product choices belong to the user. Each factual claim that affects the plan needs a path, URL, test result, or user statement.

Finish this step when each known factual dependency has evidence or an explicit unverified status.

### 3. Build the unknowns ledger

Classify each gap by the method that can expose it.

| Type | Meaning | Resolution method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Known known | A requirement or fact already stated or proven. | Record it with evidence. |
| Known unknown | A recognized unresolved decision. | Ask a focused question or propose a labeled default. |
| Unknown known | A criterion the user can recognize in examples but has not verbalized. | Show contrasting references or cheap prototypes, then record the reaction as a criterion. |
| Unknown unknown | A hidden constraint, opportunity, or failure mode that nobody has raised. | Search source, tests, documentation, prior art, and operational boundaries. |

Run a blindspot pass for unfamiliar or high-stakes territory. Record each suspected blindspot with its risk, evidence, cheapest resolution, and decision owner. Rank the items that could invalidate the plan above refinements.

When product taste remains implicit, present two or three meaningfully different references or prototypes. Use fake data and avoid wiring production systems. Convert the user's reactions into observable acceptance criteria.

Maintain a domain-language ledger when terms are fuzzy, overloaded, or inconsistent with code. Read [`references/domain-modeling-add-on.md`](references/domain-modeling-add-on.md) before creating or updating `CONTEXT.md` or an ADR.

Finish this step when every material gap has a category, owner, risk, and next resolution action.

### 4. Grill the decision tree

A grill question must pass all three tests.

| Test | Required property |
| --- | --- |
| Material | Different answers could change the implementation or its acceptance criteria. |
| Grounded | The question cites concrete evidence or a specific evidence gap. |
| Answerable | The user can select an option, approve a default, or provide a reference. |

Ask one blocking question at a time and walk the design tree branch by branch. Keep useful nonblocking questions in the session ledger. Convert low-risk gaps into labeled assumptions rather than interrupting the user.

Use this shape:

```md
Blocking question: <decision>
Why it matters: <effect of each viable answer>
Evidence: <path, document, test, or explicit gap>
Recommended answer: <default and rationale>
If you have no preference: I will use <default>.
```

Resolve questions through evidence whenever the code or documentation can answer them. Each design branch must end as resolved, explicitly assumed, or blocked.

Finish this step when no material branch remains hidden in the queue and every blocking question has one clear decision to make.

### 5. Persist the shared understanding

Update `CONTEXT.md` when domain language becomes canonical. Offer an ADR only when the decision is costly to reverse, surprising without context, and based on a real tradeoff. Keep temporary reasoning in the grill ledger rather than durable domain files.

Write or revise the implementation plan around the decision points:

| Plan section | Required content |
| --- | --- |
| Decisions | Data model, interfaces, permissions, user flows, API semantics, and migration strategy that could still change. |
| Evidence | Source and documentation that justify the approach. |
| Open questions | Remaining material unknowns, ordered by risk. |
| Assumptions | Defaults accepted for low-risk gaps. |
| References | Prototype, example, or source paths that define expected behavior. |
| Steps | Ordered implementation slices with verification gates. |
| Deviation policy | Conditions for continuing locally and conditions that require user input. |

Finish this step when an implementer can trace each consequential choice to evidence, a user decision, or a visible assumption.

### 6. Obtain build authority

Present the resolved decisions, remaining assumptions, and verification gates. Ask the user to confirm the shared understanding. If the user has already authorized implementation with labeled assumptions, record that authority in the ledger and proceed. Otherwise, continue with the next material question.

The planning phase is complete only when build authority and all accepted assumptions are explicit.

## Implementation branch

For a long-running coding-agent handoff, complete [`templates/launch-packet.md`](templates/launch-packet.md). It carries the goal, map, evidence to inspect first, unknowns, deviation policy, and verification gates. Give parallel workers distinct scopes and keep one writer per working tree.

For complex work, maintain [`templates/implementation-notes.md`](templates/implementation-notes.md). Handle deviations by impact.

| Condition | Response |
| --- | --- |
| Change is local, conservative, and low risk. | Choose the safer option, record it, and continue. |
| Change affects architecture, data migration, security, cost, or user-facing behavior. | Stop and ask the user. |
| Evidence contradicts the plan. | Follow the verified territory, update the map, and apply the impact rule above. |

After implementation, report what changed, the reason for each consequential choice, resolved unknowns, remaining assumptions, evidence, and commands or checks actually run. Add a short review checklist or quiz only when knowledge transfer is part of the request; every answer must be present in the report.

Do not modify files.</context><discovery_agent-guidelines>Focus on runtime lifecycle interfaces, workspace/worktree creation, sidecar launch and connection, terminal/file APIs, settings, schemas, cleanup, and tests. result.output:
{"backend":"headless","chat_id":"5E30194D-B6BA-48CF-8E04-266E644CE4CB","response":"The narrowest viable design is a runtime-provider abstraction with two implementations:

- Local/authenticated development: existing Podman behavior, unchanged.
- Hosted production: one persistent Fly Sprite per repository/project, containing the repository clone, all Git worktrees, workspace homes, and one long-running Node sidecar.

FastAPI and its SQLite databases remain authoritative for users, projects, workspaces, sessions, messages, and prompt journals. A small Sprite-resident agent opens an authenticated outbound WebSocket to FastAPI and exposes bounded Git, filesystem, sidecar, and terminal operations. The browser-facing API does not change.

This fits Sprites well: their ext4 filesystem persists across VM pauses, incoming work can wake a paused Sprite, they run in Firecracker microVMs, and domain-based egress policies can be updated through the API. [Fly Sprites overview](https://fly.io/sprites/)

## Recommended topology

```text
Browser
   |
   | Existing REST / prompt polling / terminal polling
   v
FastAPI + central SQLite
   |
   | authenticated multiplexed WebSocket RPC
   | project_id + request_id + operation
   v
One Sprite per repo/project
   |
   +-- /workspace/repo                  canonical checkout
   +-- /workspace/repo/.worktrees/*     multiple workspace worktrees
   +-- /workspace/homes/<workspace-id>  HOME, Pi sessions, user installs
   +-- Sprite runtime agent
   +-- Node sidecar on local Unix socket
```

Do not expose the Sprite URL publicly and do not proxy browser traffic directly to it. The outbound socket makes FastAPI the sole authorization and routing point and avoids an inbound per-project service surface.

The existing BYOC runner relay is useful precedent, but it is the wrong abstraction to reuse wholesale. Its runner registration, Noise pairing, per-runner SQLite, browser-to-runner capabilities, and worker-mode FastAPI database are designed for user-owned runners. A hosted Sprite is infrastructure owned and authenticated by Yinshi, and the central tenant database should remain authoritative.

## Runtime lifecycle

Use a new generic interface along these lines:

```python
class ProjectRuntime:
    async def ensure_project(repo_id, tenant) -> RuntimeHandle: ...
    async def request(repo_id, operation, payload) -> dict: ...
    async def open_stream(repo_id, operation, payload) -> AsyncIterator[dict]: ...
    async def touch(repo_id) -> None: ...
    async def destroy(repo_id) -> None: ...
```

Implementations:

- `PodmanRuntime`: delegates to the existing `ContainerManager` and Unix-socket sidecar behavior.
- `SpriteRuntime`: provisions/resumes the project Sprite, waits for its outbound agent connection, and dispatches RPC through it.
- Host/desktop execution continues using the current local socket and filesystem paths.

A Sprite should be created during remote repository import, or lazily on first runtime operation with a database uniqueness constraint preventing duplicates. Import should:

1. Allocate the repository ID centrally.
2. Create a stable Sprite name such as `yinshi-<deployment>-<repo-id>`.
3. Install or verify the pinned runtime bundle.
4. Configure the outbound control URL and a one-time bootstrap credential.
5. Apply the project egress policy.
6. Start the runtime agent.
7. Clone the repository inside `/workspace/repo`.
8. Mark the runtime ready only after the agent reports its version and repository state.

After that, creating a Yinshi workspace only runs `git worktree add` in that same Sprite. It must not create another Sprite or sidecar.

Pausing should be left to Sprites’ normal idle behavior. Yinshi should track connectivity and activity, but should not delete the Sprite on idle. Its filesystem will survive the pause. Explicit project deletion should revoke the connection credential, delete the Sprite, and only then remove the central project row—or record a retryable `deleting` state if Fly deletion fails.

## Sidecar and protocol

The Node sidecar should stay on a Unix socket inside the Sprite. The Sprite agent connects to it locally and forwards its existing newline-delimited messages over multiplexed RPC channels.

This avoids adding networking, authentication, or multitenancy to the sidecar itself.

The control protocol needs:

- A connection-level `hello` containing protocol version, project ID, runtime version, and bootstrap credential.
- Server-issued credential rotation after successful bootstrap.
- Request IDs and explicit operation names.
- Separate bounded request/response and streaming channels.
- Cancellation by request ID.
- Heartbeats and reconnect with exponential backoff.
- Maximum frame and in-flight request limits.
- Idempotency keys for create/delete/clone/worktree operations.
- No caller-supplied absolute paths. Operations take repository, workspace, session, and relative file IDs; the agent derives paths locally.

Core operations:

- `repo.clone`, `repo.validate`, `repo.delete`
- `worktree.create`, `worktree.restore`, `worktree.delete`
- `files.tree`, `files.changed`, `files.preview`, `files.diff`, `files.write`, `files.download`
- `sidecar.resolve_model`, `sidecar.query`, `sidecar.cancel`, `sidecar.release_session`
- `terminal.start`, `terminal.input`, `terminal.resize`, `terminal.restart`, `terminal.close`
- `runtime.health`, `runtime.version`

For prompt streaming, preserve `RunCoordinator` and `PromptJournal` centrally. Only the sidecar event source changes from a local `SidecarClient` to the project RPC stream.

For the newer polling terminal API, `TerminalJournal` should use a transport interface rather than owning a Unix socket. Its local transport preserves current behavior; its Sprite transport calls the remote terminal operations.

The old browser WebSocket terminal route can either receive the same transport abstraction or be retired after confirming no supported client uses it.

## Path model

Hosted Sprite paths should be logical and stable:

- Repository `root_path`: `/workspace/repo`
- Worktree `path`: `/workspace/repo/.worktrees/<branch>`
- Workspace home: `/workspace/homes/<workspace-id>`
- Pi session: `/workspace/homes/<workspace-id>/.yinshi/pi-sessions/<session-id>.jsonl`
- Sidecar socket: `/run/yinshi/sidecar.sock`

Central SQLite may continue returning `root_path` and `path`, but hosted code must treat them as runtime-local opaque paths. FastAPI must never call `realpath`, `open`, `git`, or `shutil` on them.

This is the main reason the current `sidecar_runtime.py` cannot simply be extended with a remote socket URL: numerous API and workspace services currently dereference those paths on the FastAPI host.

## Database changes

Both the legacy and per-tenant schemas need a project-runtime table. A separate table is cleaner than adding Fly-specific columns to `repos`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE project_runtimes (
    repo_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES repos(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    provider TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (provider IN ('podman', 'sprite')),
    external_id TEXT UNIQUE,
    status TEXT NOT NULL,
    connection_token_hash TEXT,
    runtime_version TEXT,
    last_connected_at TEXT,
    last_activity_at TEXT,
    last_error TEXT,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
```

Add an index on `status` or `last_activity_at` if a reconciliation loop will scan runtimes.

Store only a hash of the Sprite connection credential. The Fly API token remains an application secret in environment configuration, not in tenant SQLite. Do not copy the central SQLite database into each Sprite.

`root_path` and `workspaces.path` can remain required strings to minimize schema/API churn; store the runtime-local paths above.

## Exact backend files

### Must change

- `backend/src/yinshi/config.py`
  - Replace the binary hosted assumption with `execution_runtime=podman|sprite|host`.
  - Add Sprite API token, API URL, control WebSocket URL, name prefix, bootstrap version, connect timeout, and egress-policy settings.
  - Keep existing container settings for the Podman implementation.

- `.env.example`
  - Document the runtime selector and Sprite settings.
  - Clarify that `CONTAINER_ENABLED` is legacy/Podman-specific.

- `backend/src/yinshi/main.py`
  - Initialize the selected runtime manager.
  - Start the Sprite connection broker and reconciliation task in hosted mode.
  - Keep Podman initialization and destruction only in Podman mode.
  - Register the Sprite agent WebSocket route.

- `backend/src/yinshi/db.py`
  - Add `project_runtimes` to the legacy schema and migration/version handling.

- `backend/src/yinshi/tenant.py`
  - Add the same table and migration handling to every per-user database.
  - Include it in backup/migration expectations where appropriate.

- `backend/src/yinshi/models.py`
  - Add internal runtime status/provider models if lifecycle state is surfaced.
  - `RepoOut` and `WorkspaceOut` can otherwise stay unchanged.

- `backend/src/yinshi/services/sidecar_runtime.py`
  - Turn container-specific resolution into runtime-provider resolution.
  - Stop generating mounts and host-remapped paths for Sprite mode.
  - Rename generic lifecycle helpers; retain compatibility wrappers initially if desired.

- `backend/src/yinshi/services/workspace_runtime_paths.py`
  - Return logical runtime paths without host `realpath` checks in Sprite mode.
  - Delegate validation and secret-guardrail installation to the Sprite agent.

- `backend/src/yinshi/services/workspace.py`
  - Route clone repair, remote synchronization, worktree creation/restoration, and deletion through the project runtime.
  - Keep current direct Git implementation for local/Podman modes.
  - Ensure all workspaces belonging to one repo reuse its single Sprite.

- `backend/src/yinshi/api/repos.py`
  - Provision the project runtime and clone remotely on hosted import.
  - Reject hosted `local_path` imports unless an explicit upload/import flow is added.
  - Destroy the single project Sprite during repository deletion instead of destroying one container per workspace.
  - Preserve central database authorization and metadata updates.

- `backend/src/yinshi/api/workspaces.py`
  - Remove per-workspace hosted-container destruction.
  - Create/delete worktrees through the project runtime.

- `backend/src/yinshi/api/workspace_files.py`
  - Route all tree/status/preview/diff/write/download operations remotely for Sprite projects.
  - Downloads need a bounded chunk stream through RPC rather than a host file descriptor.
  - Keep the current descriptor/symlink-safe implementation for local execution.

- `backend/src/yinshi/api/stream.py`
  - Resolve the project runtime from the session’s repo.
  - Replace local Unix-socket sidecar creation with an abstract sidecar transport.
  - Remove container path remapping in Sprite mode.
  - Preserve provider resolution, central credentials, prompt journaling, cancellation, and event schemas.

## Network policy

Apply a default-deny domain policy at Sprite creation and update it from a versioned configuration.

Minimum allowlist:

- The Yinshi control-plane hostname for the outbound `wss://` connection.
- GitHub domains required for clone/fetch and GitHub API access.
- Configured AI provider API hostnames.
- Package registries explicitly supported by Yinshi, such as npm and PyPI.
- Required DNS/time/system destinations supplied by the Sprites default set.

Do not broadly allow `*.com`, arbitrary IP literals, or all port 443. Arbitrary code can still exfiltrate through any allowed destination, so the product should describe this as bounded egress, not complete data-loss prevention.

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    """Application startup and shutdown."""
    app_settings = get_settings()
    logger.info("Starting %s", app_settings.app_name)
    init_db()
    init_control_db()
    setup_oauth()

    # Per-user container isolation
    reaper_task: asyncio.Task[None] | None = None
    if app_settings.container_enabled:
        from yinshi.services.container import ContainerManager

        mgr = ContainerManager(settings=app_settings)
        await mgr.initialize()
        app.state.container_manager = mgr
        reaper_task = asyncio.create_task(mgr.run_reaper())
        logger.info("Container isolation enabled (image=%s)", app_settings.container_image)
    else:
        app.state.container_manager = None

    relay_process_lock: RelayProcessLock | None = None
    if app.state.mode == "hosted":
        relay_process_lock = RelayProcessLock(
            Path(app_settings.control_db_path).parent / "relay-process.lock"
        )
        relay_process_lock.acquire()

    try:
        yield
    finally:
        try:
            prompt_journal = getattr(app.state, "prompt_journal", None)
            if isinstance(prompt_journal, PromptJournal):
                await prompt_journal.close()
            terminal_journal = getattr(app.state, "terminal_journal", None)
            if isinstance(terminal_journal, TerminalJournal):
                await terminal_journal.close_all()
            if reaper_task:
                reaper_task.cancel()
                try:
                    await reaper_task
                except asyncio.CancelledError:
                    pass
            if app.state.container_manager:
                await app.state.container_manager.destroy_all()
        finally:
            if relay_process_lock is not None:
                relay_process_lock.release()
    logger.info("Shutdown complete")


def _configure_middleware(
    application: FastAPI,
    app_settings: Settings,
    *,
    mode: AppMode,
    worker_principal: WorkerPrincipal | None,
) -> None:
    """Attach the shared hosted middleware stack to one application instance."""
    if not isinstance(application, FastAPI):
        raise TypeError("application must be a FastAPI instance")
    if not isinstance(app_settings, Settings):
        raise TypeError("app_settings must be Settings")

    if mode == "worker":

def delete_local_pi_session_file(session_id: str) -> None:
    """Delete one durable Pi session file in legacy no-tenant mode."""
    session_directory = _local_pi_session_directory(create=False)
    session_file = os.path.join(session_directory, _pi_session_file_name(session_id))

def _pi_session_directory_is_safe_for_delete(
    home_path: Path,
    session_directory: Path,
) -> bool:
    """Return whether one Pi session directory can be safely removed."""
    if not home_path.is_absolute():
        raise ValueError("home_path must be absolute")
    if not session_directory.is_absolute():
        raise ValueError("session_directory must be absolute")

    expected_session_directory = _workspace_pi_session_directory(home_path)
    if session_directory != expected_session_directory:
        raise ValueError("session_directory must belong to home_path")

    yinshi_directory = home_path / ".yinshi"
    for path in (home_path, yinshi_directory, session_directory):
        if path.is_symlink():
            logger.warning("Refusing to delete Pi session files through a symlink")
            return False

    try:
        resolved_session_directory = session_directory.resolve(strict=False)
    except OSError:
        logger.warning("Refusing to delete Pi session files because path resolution failed")
        return False

    if resolved_session_directory != expected_session_directory:
        logger.warning("Refusing to delete Pi session files outside workspace home")
        return False

    return True


def delete_workspace_runtime_home(tenant: TenantContext, workspace_id: str) -> None:
    """Delete the complete persistent home for one workspace runtime."""
    if tenant is None:
        raise ValueError("tenant is required")
    if not workspace_id:
        raise ValueError("workspace_id must not be empty")
    home_path = _workspace_home_expected_path(tenant, workspace_id)
    runtime_directory = home_path.parent
    if not runtime_directory.exists():
        return
    if runtime_directory.is_symlink() or home_path.is_symlink():
        raise ValueError("workspace runtime path must not contain symlinks")
    if not shutil.rmtree.avoids_symlink_attacks:
        raise RuntimeError("safe descriptor-based directory deletion is unavailable")

    directory_flags = os.O_RDONLY | os.O_DIRECTORY | os.O_NOFOLLOW | os.O_CLOEXEC
    parent_fd = os.open(runtime_directory, directory_flags)
    try:
        try:
            home_stat = os.stat("home", dir_fd=parent_fd, follow_symlinks=False)
        except FileNotFoundError:
            return
        if not stat.S_ISDIR(home_stat.st_mode):
            raise ValueError("workspace home must be a directory")
        shutil.rmtree("home", dir_fd=parent_fd)
    finally:
        os.close(parent_fd)
    try:
        runtime_directory.rmdir()
    except OSError:
        logger.warning("Workspace runtime directory was not empty after cleanup")

def _append_runtime_mount(
    mounts: list[ContainerMount],
    mounts_by_target: dict[str, ContainerMount],
    *,
    source_path: str,
    target_path: str,
    read_only: bool,
) -> None:
    """Append one mount while preventing ambiguous target overlays."""
    if not os.path.isabs(source_path):
        raise ValueError("source_path must be absolute")
    if not os.path.isabs(target_path):
        raise ValueError("target_path must be absolute")

    mount = ContainerMount(
        source_path=source_path,
        target_path=target_path,
        read_only=read_only,
    )
    existing_mount = mounts_by_target.get(target_path)
    if existing_mount is not None:
        if existing_mount == mount:
            return
        raise ContainerStartError("Sidecar mount targets must be unique")

    mounts.append(mount)
    mounts_by_target[target_path] = mount


def _container_mounts_for_runtime(
    tenant: TenantContext,
    *,
    agent_dir: str | None,
    repo_root_path: str | None,
    workspace_path: str | None,
    workspace_id: str | None,
) -> tuple[ContainerMount, ...]:
    """Build the narrow mount set required by one sidecar operation."""
    mounts: list[ContainerMount] = []
    mounts_by_target: dict[str, ContainerMount] = {}
    normalized_workspace_id = _workspace_runtime_id(workspace_id)
    if normalized_workspace_id is not None:
        _append_runtime_mount(
            mounts,
            mounts_by_target,
            source_path=_workspace_home_source(tenant, normalized_workspace_id),
            target_path=_WORKSPACE_HOME_TARGET,
            read_only=False,
        )

    for source_path, read_only, mount_at_host_path in (
        (repo_root_path, False, True),
        (workspace_path, False, False),
        (agent_dir, True, False),
    ):
        if source_path is None:
            continue
        normalized_source_path = os.path.realpath(source_path)
        if not is_path_inside(normalized_source_path, tenant.data_dir):
            message = "Sidecar mount path is outside tenant data"
            raise ContainerStartError(message)
        _append_runtime_mount(
            mounts,
            mounts_by_target,
            source_path=normalized_source_path,
            target_path=remap_path_for_container(
                normalized_source_path,
                tenant.data_dir,
            ),
            read_only=read_only,
        )
        if mount_at_host_path:
            # Git worktrees store absolute gitdir pointers into the repo's
            # metadata. Mounting the repo at that same absolute path lets Git
            # resolve those pointers inside the sidecar while cwd stays in
            # /data.
            _append_runtime_mount(
                mounts,
                mounts_by_target,
                source_path=normalized_source_path,
                target_path=normalized_source_path,
                read_only=read_only,
            )
    return tuple(mounts)


async def resolve_tenant_sidecar_context(
    request: Request,
    tenant: TenantContext | None,
    runtime_session_id: str | None = None,
    repo_agents_md: str | None = None,
    repo_root_path: str | None = None,
    workspace_path: str | None = None,
    workspace_id: str | None = None,
) -> TenantSidecarContext:
    """Resolve the socket path and Pi runtime inputs for one request."""
    if tenant is None:
        return TenantSidecarContext(
            socket_path=None,
            agent_dir=None,
            settings_payload=None,
        )

    settings = get_settings()
    runtime_inputs = resolve_effective_pi_runtime(
        tenant.user_id,
        tenant.data_dir,
        runtime_session_id=runtime_session_id,
        repo_agents_md=repo_agents_md,
    )
    narrow_mounts = settings.container_mount_mode == "narrow"
    runtime_id = _workspace_runtime_id(workspace_id)
    pi_session_file = None
    if runtime_session_id is not None and workspace_id is not None:
        pi_session_file = _workspace_pi_session_runtime_file(
            tenant,
            workspace_id,
            runtime_session_id,
            container_enabled=settings.container_enabled,
            narrow_mounts=narrow_mounts,
        )
    runtime_agent_dir = _resolve_agent_dir_for_runtime(
        runtime_inputs.agent_dir,
        tenant.data_dir,
        container_enabled=settings.container_enabled,
    )

    if not settings.container_enabled:
        return TenantSidecarContext(
            socket_path=None,
            agent_dir=runtime_agent_dir,
            settings_payload=runtime_inputs.settings_payload,
            runtime_id=runtime_id,
            pi_session_file=pi_session_file,
        )

    container_manager = getattr(request.app.state, "container_manager", None)
    if container_manager is None:
        raise ContainerStartError("Container manager is not initialized")

    container_mounts = None
    if narrow_mounts:
        container_mounts = _container_mounts_for_runtime(
            tenant,
            agent_dir=runtime_inputs.agent_dir,
            repo_root_path=repo_root_path,
            workspace_path=workspace_path,
            workspace_id=runtime_id,
        )
    container_info = await container_manager.ensure_container(
        tenant.user_id,
        tenant.data_dir,
        mounts=container_mounts,
        runtime_id=runtime_id,
        environment=workspace_runtime_environment(runtime_id),
    )
    return TenantSidecarContext(
        socket_path=container_info.socket_path,
        agent_dir=runtime_agent_dir,
        settings_payload=runtime_inputs.settings_payload,
        runtime_id=runtime_id,
        pi_session_file=pi_session_file,
    )


def _call_container_method(
    method: object,
    user_id: str,
    *args: object,
    runtime_id: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    """Call a container manager lifecycle method for one runtime."""
    if not callable(method):
        return
    method(user_id, *args, runtime_id=runtime_id)


@asynccontextmanager
async def tenant_container_activity(
    request: Request,
    tenant: TenantContext | None,
    *,
    runtime_id: str | None = None,
    protect_lease_key: str | None = None,
    protect_timeout_s: int | None = None,
) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
    """Mark a container busy, then optionally keep it alive after work ends."""
    if protect_lease_key is not None and protect_timeout_s is None:
        raise ValueError("protect_timeout_s is required when protect_lease_key is set")
    if protect_timeout_s is not None and protect_timeout_s < 0:
        raise ValueError("protect_timeout_s must not be negative")

    begin_tenant_container_activity(request, tenant, runtime_id=runtime_id)
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        end_tenant_container_activity(request, tenant, runtime_id=runtime_id)
        if protect_lease_key is not None:
            assert protect_timeout_s is not None, "protect timeout must be validated"
            protect_tenant_container(
                request,
                tenant,
                lease_key=protect_lease_key,
                timeout_s=protect_timeout_s,
                runtime_id=runtime_id,
            )

    if container_manager is None or user_id is None:

    _call_container_method(
        getattr(container_manager, "touch", None), user_id, runtime_id=runtime_id

    _call_container_method(
        getattr(container_manager, "begin_activity", None),

def end_tenant_container_activity(

def protect_tenant_container(
    request: Request,
    tenant: TenantContext | None,
    *,
    lease_key: str,
    timeout_s: int,
    runtime_id: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    """Keep one tenant container alive for a named long-lived operation."""
    container_manager, user_id = _tenant_container_manager(request, tenant)
    if container_manager is None or user_id is None:
        return
    _call_container_method(
        getattr(container_manager, "protect", None),

def release_tenant_container(
    request: Request,
    tenant: TenantContext | None,
    *,

    """Remove one named long-lived keepalive lease from a tenant container."""
    container_manager, user_id = _tenant_container_manager(request, tenant)
    if container_manager is None or user_id is None:
        return
    _call_container_method(
        getattr(container_manager, "unprotect", None),

def _tenant_container_manager(
    request: Request,
    tenant: TenantContext | None,
) -> tuple[object | None, str | None]:
    """Return the container manager plus tenant user id when container mode is active."""
    if tenant is None:

def _fetch_repo(db: sqlite3.Connection, repo_id: str) -> sqlite3.Row:
    """Load a repo row or raise RepoNotFoundError."""
    assert repo_id, "repo_id must not be empty"
    repo = db.execute("SELECT * FROM repos WHERE id = ?", (repo_id,)).fetchone()
    if not repo:
        raise RepoNotFoundError(f"Repo {repo_id} not found")
    return cast(sqlite3.Row, repo)


def _fetch_workspace(db: sqlite3.Connection, workspace_id: str) -> sqlite3.Row:
    """Load a workspace row or raise WorkspaceNotFoundError."""
    assert workspace_id, "workspace_id must not be empty"
    workspace = db.execute(
        "SELECT * FROM workspaces WHERE id = ?",
        (workspace_id,),
    ).fetchone()
    if not workspace:
        raise WorkspaceNotFoundError(f"Workspace {workspace_id} not found")
    return cast(sqlite3.Row, workspace)


def _tenant_path_is_trusted(tenant: TenantContext, path: str) -> bool:
    """Return whether a tenant path is inside tenant-managed storage."""
    assert tenant.data_dir, "tenant.data_dir must not be empty"
    assert path, "path must not be empty"
    if is_path_inside(path, tenant.data_dir):
        return True

    settings = get_settings()
    if settings.container_enabled:
        return False
    if settings.allowed_repo_base and is_path_inside(path, settings.allowed_repo_base):
        return True
    return False

    assert repo_id, "repo_id must not be empty"
    return os.path.join(tenant.data_dir, "repos", repo_id)
